passage: From behind the shop counter, Tejas watched his son Hrithik: twenty-five, back in their small town for the third time in two years, this time after leaving a call-centre job in Pune. At that age Tejas had been married, running this hardware shop and paying off the loan. The neighbours had started asking. At dinner he nearly said, "When will you settle?" He had said it before, and it had ended with a slammed door. Instead he tore a roti and asked, "What did you like in Pune, and what did you hate?" Hrithik looked up, surprised. "Liked the training part. Hated the night shifts." "Hmm. And next?" "Maybe teaching computers. I'm checking the institute in town." Tejas nodded slowly. It wasn't the life he'd had. Maybe it didn't need to be.

qa.q: What job had Hrithik left in Pune?
qa.a: A call-centre job.

qa.q: What was Tejas worried about as he watched Hrithik?
qa.a: He worried Hrithik wasn't settling, since at that age Tejas had been married and running the shop, and the neighbours were asking.

qa.q: Why did asking what he liked and hated work better than "When will you settle?"
qa.a: It invited Hrithik to share instead of defend himself, which avoided another slammed door and brought out his plan to teach computers.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when his father asks a question instead of passing a verdict?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and respected, and more willing to talk about what comes next.

grounding: A father worried by his mid-twenties son's return home and job changes chooses to ask questions instead of passing judgment.

passage: Santiago found the note on the fridge again: Back late, interview. Marek was twenty-six, living in the room he had grown up in, and this would be his fourth job since university. At twenty-six Santiago had already bought this Madrid flat with Marek's mother. At the bakery where he worked, his colleague Lucía laughed when he complained. "Mine is twenty-eight and still at home. Rents are madness now. It's not the road we walked." That evening Marek came in, tired. Santiago swallowed "Another job?" and set two plates on the table instead. "How did it go? What are you looking for this time?" Marek sat down slowly. "Somewhere I can actually learn, Papá. Not just survive." Santiago nodded. He still worried. But he asked another question instead of giving a speech.

qa.q: What did the note on the fridge say?
qa.a: Back late, interview.

qa.q: What was Santiago worried about?
qa.a: That Marek, at twenty-six, was still living at home and on his fourth job, when Santiago had bought a flat by that age.

qa.q: What helped Santiago ask questions instead of giving a speech?
qa.a: Lucía's reminder that rents are madness and it's not the same road helped him see Marek's path as different, not failing.

qa.q: How might Marek feel when his father asks what he is looking for?
qa.a: He may feel taken seriously rather than judged, which lets him explain that he wants somewhere to learn.

grounding: A father worried about his twenty-six-year-old son living at home and changing jobs learns the path is longer now and asks questions instead of lecturing.

passage: In the queue at the district records office, Ganga watched her son Farhan fill in the form for his transcript. Twenty-five, still in his old room at home, now leaving his second job to study animation. Her sister had said on the phone, "He's drifting, Ganga. Put your foot down." The words had sat in her chest all week. But here Farhan was, checking every box twice, chatting politely with the clerk, fixing a wrong date without fuss. She realised she had never asked him what the course actually involved. On the bus home, she did. "What will you make in the first year?" Farhan turned, surprised, and talked for twenty minutes about storyboards. Ganga still worried about the fees. But she saw a young man choosing, not drifting, and she told him so.

qa.q: Where were Ganga and Farhan queuing?
qa.a: At the district records office.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel after her sister called Farhan drifting?
qa.a: The words sat in her chest all week, leaving her anxious that her son was going nowhere.

qa.q: What turning point on the bus changed how Ganga saw Farhan?
qa.a: She asked what he'd make in the first year, and his twenty minutes on storyboards showed a plan, not drifting.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when his mother says she sees him choosing?
qa.a: He'd likely feel respected and encouraged, since her worry didn't turn into a verdict 🙂

grounding: A mother worried about her twenty-five-year-old son at home and changing course asks about his plans instead of passing a verdict.

passage:
Dear Imtiaz,
I'm leaving this on your desk because when we talk, I end up sounding like your Nani did with me.
When you moved back home in March, I told my friends you were "between things". I lay awake doing sums: at twenty-five I was married, working at the bank, with a baby on the way. You have changed jobs three times. I worried you were lost.
Then Rehana at work said her son's path looked just like yours, and she showed me an article saying most young people take longer to settle now. Maybe the road is simply longer than mine was.
So instead of a verdict, I have questions. What did you like in each job? What do you want the next one to have? And is there anything you need from me, other than silence at dinner?
With love and a little less worry,
Your Ammi, Ritu

qa.q: When did Imtiaz move back home?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: What was Ritu worried about as she lay awake doing sums?
qa.a: She worried Imtiaz was lost, comparing three job changes with her own life at twenty-five.

qa.q: What turning point changed Ritu's approach, and what does she do instead?
qa.a: Rehana's story and the article about longer paths made her swap a verdict for questions about what Imtiaz liked and wants next.

qa.q: How might Imtiaz feel finding questions on the desk instead of a lecture?
qa.a: Imtiaz may feel respected rather than judged, and more willing to talk than to sit in silence at dinner.

grounding: A mother worried about her twenty-five-year-old living at home and changing jobs realises paths are longer now and chooses questions over verdicts.

passage:
You asked why Vikas and I stopped fighting, Rashmi? Sit, I'll tell you.
Vikas is twenty-six. Four jobs in three years: a bank, a startup that shut, a travel company, now something with maps. And still in the room with the cricket posters. Every Sunday I'd say, "At your age your father and I had a flat and a child." Every Sunday a door would bang.
Then one night I couldn't sleep, and I actually read his CV. In every job he'd learned one thing and carried it forward. The maps job uses all of it. It wasn't drifting. It was a longer road than ours, with more turns.
Now on Sundays I ask one question instead: "What are you learning this month?" Last week he talked for an hour. He's still at home. I still worry sometimes. But I'm Kashish the mother again, not Kashish the judge.

qa.q: How many jobs has Vikas had in three years?
qa.a: Four jobs in three years.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel when she read Vikas's CV?
qa.a: She felt reassured, seeing that he had learned one thing in every job and carried it forward, so it was a longer road, not drifting.

qa.q: What question did Kashish start asking, and why did it work?
qa.a: 'What are you learning this month?', which invited him to explain instead of defend himself, so he talked for an hour.

qa.q: What might Sunday dinners have felt like for Vikas before the change?
qa.a: They probably felt like a weekly verdict on his life, which is why a door banged every time.

grounding: A mother worried by her son's job changes and life at home comes to see a longer, non-linear path and starts asking questions instead of giving verdicts.
